doc.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Shinagawa quartermaster depot club and where the camps were
summary: Brown pins down the Shinagawa location and the unknown camps; she recalls that the club's audience was mostly black soldiers.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: You said, where was it? Shinagawa?

Shinagawa. And there was a … today Shinagawa … today, it‟s the east side, which is the ocean side, there was nothing there. Today it is the most hip place. Even Dean & Deluca has a store [there]. It‟s like a really upscale, and uh, [as] famous here as the Oyster Bar in the station, [Grand] Central Station, they have a restaurant over there, the east side. But in those days there was nothing there. And then, from that side, there was this club.
And the name of the club again?

I don‟t remember. As I said, this club is the … the Ichiban Octet—I don‟t even know if it had a name, because it was for the Americans, as I said, it was all black musicians, I mean, excuse me, troops.…
Soldiers. Every once in a while I saw white soldiers, but it could‟ve been a sergeants‟ club, I‟m not quite sure. But it was something to do with shipping, something depot.
Now, you mentioned a club, or a camp before, was that Camp Zama that you ….
…said the truck used to come and get you? What was that? Remember, you said you guys would wait for the truck to come and get you and take you to a camp?
I have no idea where they were.
But I know it was in Tokyo. And as I mentioned, I said it would go from one place to another sometimes.
So, I‟m not quite sure where they were. I have no idea. I don‟t even know where Zama is even today.
